extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of moral philosophy; readers of Schopenhauer and classical philosophical texts
extracted.subtask_description: Expository chapter on ethics within Schopenhauer's pessimistic metaphysics: claims about the nature of pleasure and pain, the justification (or lack) of the world, and the proper subject-matter and foundations of moral inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure as mere negation; pain as positive
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure is merely negative and therefore often unperceived while possessed; pain is positive and makes itself felt — hence we become conscious of blessings only after losing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and consequences given: health, youth, and freedom are noticed only after loss; the more pleasures increase the less susceptible we become to them; time becomes noticeable when bored; great joy is conceived as consequence of prior great misery; poets must bring heroes into suffering to free them and produce joy (arts depend on suffering).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare total possible pleasures vs total possible sorrows
rubrics_metrics.description: Before asserting life is worth desiring, one must calmly compare the sum of possible pleasures a man can enjoy with the sum of possible sorrows which may come to him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author claims the balance is decided by the mere existence of evil because evil cannot be annulled or balanced by good; even many pleasures cannot outweigh a single torment (Petrarch: 'A thousand pleasures are not worth one torment').

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of any evil suffices to render the world's existence undesirable
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere existence of evil decides that non-existence would be preferable to existence; the presence of any suffering cannot be undone by other goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by quotations (Voltaire, Byron) and argument that past suffering is not undone by later well-being; therefore one has reason to mourn existence rather than rejoice in it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimism is unjustified and pernicious
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic optimism (the thesis that this is the best of all possible worlds) is a sophistical and pernicious doctrine, an 'unmerited self-praise' of the will to live that misrepresents life as desirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments: optimism conflicts with the manifest misery of the world and with Christianity; historical critique of Leibnitz and theodicies; Voltaire's 'Candide' and Hume's works used as exemplars of anti-optimistic rebuttal.

rubrics_metrics.name: This world is the worst possible world that can continue to exist
rubrics_metrics.description: The world is as bad as it can be while still being able to maintain itself; a slightly worse world could not continue, hence our world is the worst of the possible worlds that can exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support: examples from planetary stability, catastrophes (Lisbon, Haiti, Pompeii), disease, and the precarious conditions of animal and human life; fossil records as evidence of past 'worse' worlds that ceased to continue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral investigations concern the thing-in-itself (will) and are more difficult
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral (ethical) investigations are incomparably more difficult than physical ones because they almost immediately concern the thing in itself — the will — rather than merely phenomena/ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical truths remain in the province of the idea/phenomenon; moral consideration alone can offer consolation because it reveals inner nature (will).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics gains full rights only if man’s true nature is will
rubrics_metrics.description: Only if the true nature of man is his own will can ethics be accorded its complete rights; otherwise deeds would trace back to another origin and moral responsibility would not properly belong to the agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulated as 'operari sequitur esse' — the moral assessment of deeds follows from the being of the agent; if agents are not self-originating, guilt or credit reverts to the originator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics is concerned with willing (the individual's inner will), not merely actions or results
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper material for ethics is willing itself; willing occurs only in the individual, so moral evaluation must focus on the individual's will rather than on actions' external results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads to the claim that ethical judgement should prioritize inner disposition over aggregate consequences; supports focusing on individuals rather than collectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics should focus on the individual rather than nations or masses
rubrics_metrics.description: In every individual appears the whole undivided will to live; the microcosm is like the macrocosm — nations (masses) are mere abstractions and have no more moral content than individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequent claim: it is perverse to make the conduct of nations the material of ethics; moral decisions are about individuals, not the fate of nations (which are phenomena).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pantheism undermines the possibility of ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Pantheism (and revived Spinozism) ultimately overthrows ethics because if nature/the world is divine, then all that happens is 'equally divine and excellent', leaving nothing truly censurable or praiseworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spinoza is criticised for explaining right and wrong as conventional; the revival of pantheism leads to shallow, philistine moral instruction; ethical demands inevitably refute pantheistic positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral order must correspond to the will that produces the world
rubrics_metrics.description: The force that produces the phenomenon of the world (the will) determines its nature; therefore the phenomenon of the will must correspond to its moral nature, connecting moral order of the world with the productive force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference to prior work ('Ueber den Willen in der Natur') and to an exposition of 'eternal justice' (§§ 63 and 64) as underpinning a moral tendency in the world's phenomenon.
